newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: APEC to push freer fund flows, comment on currencies.
newsitem.headline: APEC to push freer fund flows, comment on currencies.

text.p: Asia Pacific finance ministers were set on Sunday to endorse proposals to help attract more than $1 trillion for development and to say currency exchange rate misalignments had been corrected, officials said.
The fund flow proposals centre around more uniform regulation among members, transparency and availability of information, easing the ability to invest internationally, and liberalising markets.

"There's a consensus that the idea of opening up, liberalisation, private sector participation is the way to go," Philippine Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo, chairman of the meeting here of top financial officials of the 18-member APEC, told reporters on Saturday.
But, he added: "Nobody is forcing anybody to do it along any particular timing. Everybody has his own timing and it is recognised by everybody."
On currencies, the ministers will state that major currency misalignments, which could have negative effects on countries' trade and economic situations, have been corrected.

That is something the powerful Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations has been saying, as the communique is specifically expected to note, and could be seen as an endorsement of exchange rates roughly around current levels.
"Asian economies are a large enough part of the world that there should be a common understanding on exchange rates," one Japanese official said.

A delegate had said on Saturday the reference on currencies would be the first of its kind. However, last year's meeting communique had noted rate fluctuations which did not reflect fundamentals had begun to reverse, without referring to the G7.
Other sources said the communique would also call for completion by the end of the year of worldwide negotiations on liberalising financial services.

The finance ministers' weekend meeting at a luxury resort hotel here has been upbeat despite some inevitable differences given member economies' varying stages of development, Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin told reporters.
"There was a general feeling we're going beyond the principle and that it really is time for action," he said.

In a media briefing on Saturday, an advisory group of APEC private financiers listed a series of concrete steps they wanted member governments to take -- from establishment of regional information centres on financing needs to creation of bond rating agncies.

The aim: to attract an estimated $1.5 trillion developing economies of the region will need in the next decade to build telecommunication links, roads and other infrastructure vital to a modern economy.

"There is no point for any economy to start talking about being a tiger economy when the growl of the tiger cannot be heard because it would take 10 calls between two telephone companies," said Johnny Ravalo, chief economist of the Bankers Association f the Philippines.
Many of the financiers' recommendations involved steps to promote development of fully fledged capital markets throughout the region.
"The development of domestic bond markets is viewed as essential," the financiers said. "This voluntary initiative must be treated as a priority."
The financiers also complained of the treatment global bank regulators accord developing country debt.

Those regulations, which determine how much and what type of capital banks must set aside to cover their loans, mean the cost of capital for developing country borowers is five times more than for their industrial country counterparts, Ravalo said.
Among the financiers' other recommendations: cross listing of securities on various stock markets and standardization of accounting principles that companies must follow.

APEC, the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, comprises Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and the Unite States.
